title: Unseen poetry: analysing one poem
specPoints: Paper 2 Section C: unseen poetry, Question 27.1
AO1 response to the poem; AO2 methods

tips.title: 24 marks, AO1 and AO2
tips.body: Question 27.1 has no AO3. Stay with the words on the page; guesses about the poet earn nothing.

tips.title: Find the turn
tips.body: Every poem changes somewhere. In Adlestrop it is And for that minute. Build the answer round the before and after.

tips.title: Small words, big effects
tips.body: Unwontedly; only; and; farther. A fine-grained answer reads single words.

tips.title: Tentative is strong
tips.body: Perhaps, might, could be read: exploration of more than one meaning, not a sign of weakness.

tips.title: Three passes, not one
tips.body: Read for the situation, then for the turn, then for methods: rushing straight to naming techniques misses where the poem changes and why.

why.matters: Most poems you meet in life are unseen: in a newspaper, a card, on a wall, at a funeral. The unseen question tests whether you can read any poem on your own, finding its situation, its turn and its methods, and saying what it means with evidence. The skill is the same for every text, which is why it is worth practising on poems you will never be examined on.

examples.title: A poem at a funeral or a wedding
examples.body: Poems are read aloud at the moments that matter most, and most listeners have never seen them before. Hearing where a poem turns, and what its last line does, is how a listener understands it at once.

examples.title: Reading closely anywhere
examples.body: Lawyers, editors and advertisers read single words closely because a single word can change a meaning. Unwontedly and only do that in Adlestrop, and noticing them is the same skill.

steps.title: The unseen question: 24 marks and 8
steps.body:
Paper 2 Section C prints two poems you have not studied. The specification says students answer one question on one unseen poem and one question comparing it with a second.

**Question 27.1: 24 marks, AO1 12 and AO2 12.** How does the poet present a named idea in the first poem? There is no AO3 here: context is not assessed, and you are not expected to know anything about the poet.

**Question 27.2: 8 marks, AO2 only.** The similarities and differences between the methods the two poets use.

**June 2024.** Question 27.1 asked how the poet of *The washing never gets done* presents ideas about daily life and connecting with the natural world; 27.2 compared its methods with those of *A Day in Autumn*. Both are modern poems in copyright, so these topics practise on poems now out of copyright.

**Time.** Section C is 32 of the paper's 96 marks: about 35 minutes for 27.1 and 10 for 27.2.

steps.title: The poem: Adlestrop
steps.body:
Read this poem by Edward Thomas as if it were on the exam paper: twice, slowly, pen in hand.

> Yes. I remember Adlestrop--\
> The name, because one afternoon\
> Of heat the express-train drew up there\
> Unwontedly. It was late June.
>
> The steam hissed. Someone cleared his throat.\
> No one left and no one came\
> On the bare platform. What I saw\
> Was Adlestrop--only the name
>
> And willows, willow-herb, and grass,\
> And meadowsweet, and haycocks dry,\
> No whit less still and lonely fair\
> Than the high cloudlets in the sky.
>
> And for that minute a blackbird sang\
> Close by, and round him, mistier,\
> Farther and farther, all the birds\
> Of Oxfordshire and Gloucestershire.

**First reading: the situation.** A train stops at a small country station on a hot afternoon. Nobody gets on or off. The speaker sees the name, the plants, the sky, and hears a blackbird, then all the birds of two counties.

**Second reading: the shape.** It begins with a memory, *I remember*; it narrows to one silent platform; it widens at the end, farther and farther, to the whole countryside. Find where the poem turns: at *And for that minute*.

steps.title: Methods: sentences, silence and lists
steps.body:
**Short sentences and caesura.** “The steam hissed. Someone cleared his throat.”: two short sentences in one line, with a full stop in the middle. The sounds are tiny, and the silence around them is large. “It was late June.”

**Enjambment.** The train “one afternoon Of heat the express-train drew up there Unwontedly”: the sentence runs over the line end, as the train runs on and then stops.

**Negatives.** “No one left and no one came” “On the bare platform”. What does not happen is the event.

**Lists.** “And willows, willow-herb, and grass, And meadowsweet, and haycocks dry”: plain nouns joined by *and*, as if the speaker had time to notice everything.

**Expansion.** “mistier, Farther and farther, all the birds” “Of Oxfordshire and Gloucestershire”. The last line is almost all place names, spreading out like the sound.

steps.body: A question in the exam's shape: *In 'Adlestrop', how does the poet present a moment of stillness?*

visuals.problem: Write a paragraph on how the ending presents the moment.

steps.text: The idea: Thomas presents stillness as a kind of listening, in which the smallest sound opens a whole landscape.
The turn: “And for that minute a blackbird sang Close by”. The time is exact and short, and the singer is near.
The widening: round him, “mistier, Farther and farther, all the birds”.

steps.text: The last line: “Of Oxfordshire and Gloucestershire”. Two county names fill it, so the poem ends in space rather than in the station.

steps.text: The effect: the minute of stillness is remembered because, in it, the speaker heard the whole country.

steps.title: AO1: a response, not a summary
steps.body:
AO1 in Section C asks for a response to task and text, with references to support interpretation.

**Answer the question's focus.** If it asks about stillness, every paragraph is about stillness.

**Interpret.** Say what the poem means to you, and why: *the memory survives because nothing happened*.

**Tentative language.** You have not studied the poem, and the examiner knows it. *Perhaps*, *this might suggest*, *the poem could be read as* show thought.

**No context, no guesses.** You are not told about the poet and are not rewarded for guessing. Stay with the words on the page.

steps.title: A method for 35 minutes
steps.body:
A routine for 27.1, so the poem is read, not rushed.

1. **Read the question first,** then the poem twice. Underline the focus.
2. **The situation in a sentence.** Who speaks, where, what happens.
3. **The shape.** Where the poem turns; how it begins and ends.
4. **Four or five moments,** each with a method and an effect on the focus.
5. **An idea,** one sentence that the paragraphs serve.
6. **Write:** idea; three or four paragraphs following the poem's shape; a last sentence on the ending.

About five minutes to read and plan, twenty-five to write, five to check.

steps.title: Annotate the middle of the poem
steps.body:
Take the question *In 'Adlestrop', how does the poet present a moment of stillness?* and work on stanzas two and three.

1. Find two negatives in stanza two, and say what each makes the reader notice.
2. Find the list in stanza three. Why *and* so many times?
3. What does *only the name* suggest about the place?
4. What is compared with the flowers and grass in the last two lines of stanza three?

Then write a paragraph on stillness in the middle of the poem.

steps.title: Level 6: critical, exploratory, fine-grained
steps.body:
The Level 6 descriptor for Question 27 asks for a critical, exploratory, conceptualised response to task and text, judicious references, and fine-grained, insightful analysis of methods with subject terminology used judiciously.

**Conceptualised.** One idea about the focus that the whole answer serves: *stillness as listening*.

**Fine-grained.** Not *there is imagery* but what one word does: *Unwontedly* makes the stop unusual, and so worth remembering; *only* reduces the place to a name.

**Structure.** Follow the poem's shape: memory, stillness, turn, widening.

**Exploratory.** Offer a second reading: the minute could be peace itself, precious because it is brief. Many readers know the train stopped in June 1914, weeks before the First World War, and that Thomas was killed in 1917; the exam does not ask for that, and the answer should not need it.

steps.title: Analysing one poem in one page
steps.body:
Question 27.1: one unseen poem, 24 marks, AO1 and AO2.

- **The question:** how does the poet present a named idea; no context; about 35 minutes.
- **Read:** twice; the situation; the turn; the beginning and the end.
- **Methods:** sentences and caesura, enjambment, negatives, lists, comparisons, how the poem widens or narrows.
- **AO1:** the focus in every paragraph; interpret; tentative language; no guesses about the poet.
- **Level 6:** one idea; fine-grained reading of single words; the poem's structure followed; a second reading offered.
- **Practised on:** Adlestrop, a moment of stillness that opens into the whole countryside.

questions.prompt:
Read the poem, then answer the question.

> Yes. I remember Adlestrop--\
> The name, because one afternoon\
> Of heat the express-train drew up there\
> Unwontedly. It was late June.
>
> The steam hissed. Someone cleared his throat.\
> No one left and no one came\
> On the bare platform. What I saw\
> Was Adlestrop--only the name
>
> And willows, willow-herb, and grass,\
> And meadowsweet, and haycocks dry,\
> No whit less still and lonely fair\
> Than the high cloudlets in the sky.
>
> And for that minute a blackbird sang\
> Close by, and round him, mistier,\
> Farther and farther, all the birds\
> Of Oxfordshire and Gloucestershire.

In 'Adlestrop', how does the poet present a moment of stillness? Write an opening idea and two paragraphs.
questions.solution:
Thomas presents stillness as a kind of listening, in which the smallest sounds make a silence large enough to hear a whole landscape. The poem begins in memory, “Yes. I remember Adlestrop”, and the reason for remembering is that the train stopped “one afternoon Of heat the express-train drew up there Unwontedly”: the unusual word marks the moment as out of the ordinary. The stillness is made of tiny sounds, “The steam hissed. Someone cleared his throat.”, two short sentences divided by a caesura, and of absences, “No one left and no one came” “On the bare platform”. Perhaps what the speaker remembers is exactly that nothing happened. He saw “only the name”, and then, with time to look, “And willows, willow-herb, and grass, And meadowsweet, and haycocks dry”, each plant added with *and* as if the eye were moving slowly along the bank.

The poem turns at “And for that minute a blackbird sang Close by”. The minute is exact and brief, and the singer is near; but the song opens outwards, “mistier, Farther and farther, all the birds”, until the final line is made almost entirely of place names, “Of Oxfordshire and Gloucestershire”. The structure moves from a silent platform to a whole countryside, and so the stillness becomes spacious rather than empty: it is the silence in which, for one minute, the speaker could hear everything.

Choose two single words in 'Adlestrop' and write a fine-grained paragraph on what each contributes to the poem's presentation of the moment.
questions.solution: *Unwontedly* and *only* carry the poem's idea in two words. *Unwontedly*, in “one afternoon Of heat the express-train drew up there Unwontedly”, means unusually, against habit: an express does not normally stop at a small station, and the long, formal adverb, set alone at the start of a line by enjambment, makes the stop feel like an event. It explains why the memory exists at all. *Only*, in “only the name”, does the opposite work: it reduces the place to a sign on a platform. The speaker never saw the village; the poem is built from almost nothing, a name, a minute, a bird. Together the two words make the moment both rare and slight, which is why, perhaps, it lasted in his mind.

examTechnique.body:
**27.1: 24 marks, AO1 12, AO2 12.** No context.

**Read twice, find the turn.** Build the answer on the poem's shape.

**Methods with effects on the focus.** Sentences, caesura, enjambment, lists, images, endings.

**About 35 minutes,** leaving 10 for 27.2.
examinerErrors: Summarising the poem line by line.
Guessing at the poet's life or context, which earns nothing.
Spending so long on 27.1 that 27.2 is rushed.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer to 27.1 opens with one idea about the focus, follows the poem's structure to its turn and ending, reads single words finely, uses terminology judiciously, and offers interpretations tentatively, all from the page.
